questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code daily for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation in a shared repository, and you own how it is configured for the whole team.
questions.stem: During a session, the tech lead types: "Remember that the contract tests only pass when the mock payment gateway is running via docker compose up gateway-mock." Claude replies that it saved a memory, and for the rest of the week it starts the mock gateway correctly for her. Her teammates, working in the same repository on their own laptops, keep getting failing contract tests because Claude never starts it for them. The lead wants this fact to reach everyone, now and for future hires, with the least ongoing effort. What should she do?

options.text: Ask every teammate to tell Claude the same sentence in their own sessions so that each machine saves its own local copy of the memory.
Add the mock-gateway requirement to the project CLAUDE.md, via /memory or a direct edit, and commit it to the repository.
Copy her ~/.claude/projects/ memory folder for this repository into the repo so that teammates' sessions can find and load it.
Set autoMemoryEnabled to true in the committed .claude/settings.json so that the memory Claude saved is enabled in every teammate's sessions.

questions.explanation: Asking Claude to "remember" something saves it to **auto memory**, which lives under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` on that one machine. It never travels through version control, so only the lead benefits. Facts the whole team needs belong in the **project CLAUDE.md**, which is committed and loaded for everyone who clones the repo. The docs say to ask Claude directly to "add this to CLAUDE.md" or edit the file through `/memory` when you want an instruction there instead of in auto memory.

whyWrong.A: This works only for people who remember to do it, has to be repeated for every new hire, and leaves each machine with its own local copy that can drift.
whyWrong.C: Auto memory is read from the user's home directory, not from a folder inside the repository, so copying it into the repo does not make it load. It is also the wrong tool for shared, reviewed team configuration.
whyWrong.D: autoMemoryEnabled only switches the feature on or off. The memory files themselves stay machine-local under each developer's home directory, so nothing the lead's Claude learned reaches anyone else.

questions.mindset: Team knowledge goes in committed project memory; "remember this" only teaches your own machine.

questions.stem: A team's project CLAUDE.md contains lines such as "Write clean code", "Test your changes" and "Keep files organized". Claude follows them inconsistently: sometimes it runs the tests, sometimes not, and new API handlers end up in different folders. The team wants the MOST effective change to make Claude's behavior consistent without adding tooling. What should they do?

options.text: Rewrite the same three lines in capital letters and prefix each one with IMPORTANT so that Claude treats them as higher priority than other context.
Add several long examples of well-structured code from the repository under each rule so that Claude can infer what each one means.
Replace each vague line with a concrete, checkable one, such as "Run npm test before committing" and "API handlers live in src/api/handlers/."
Switch the team's default model to the largest available model so that it interprets the existing high-level guidance more reliably.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration, so how instructions are written matters. The docs advise writing instructions that are **concrete enough to verify**: "Run `npm test` before committing" instead of "Test your changes", or "API handlers live in `src/api/handlers/`" instead of "Keep files organized". Vague lines leave Claude to guess what the team means, which produces exactly this inconsistency.

whyWrong.A: Emphasis does not tell Claude what "clean" or "organized" means here. The instruction is still ambiguous, just louder.
whyWrong.B: Long examples add a lot of context to every session and still leave Claude to infer the rule. A one-line concrete instruction is cheaper and clearer.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model cannot recover information that is not in the instruction. The problem is underspecified guidance, not model capability.

questions.mindset: Write CLAUDE.md rules so a reviewer could check whether they were followed.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code daily for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation in a shared repository, and you own how it is configured for the whole team.
questions.stem: Last year the team moved from Jest to Vitest; the migration is complete and no Jest tests remain. The root CLAUDE.md was updated to say "Write tests with Vitest." An older file, .claude/rules/testing.md, which has no paths frontmatter, still says "Use Jest for all unit tests." Claude now switches between the two frameworks from one task to the next. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Add a line to the root CLAUDE.md saying that when two instructions conflict, Claude must always prefer the root CLAUDE.md over any rules file.
Add paths frontmatter to testing.md so that the Jest rule loads only when Claude works on files in the older test directories of the repository.
Add a PreToolUse hook that rejects any edit importing from jest, so that Claude is forced to pick Vitest whenever it writes a new test.
Remove or update the outdated Jest instruction in testing.md so that every loaded instruction file agrees on the test framework.

questions.explanation: Unscoped rules load at launch with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so Claude sees both statements in every session. The docs warn that when two instructions contradict each other, **Claude may pick one arbitrarily**, and recommend periodically reviewing CLAUDE.md files, nested CLAUDE.md files and `.claude/rules/` to remove outdated or conflicting instructions (`/doctor prompt-audit` can find them for you). Fixing the stale line removes the root cause.

whyWrong.A: A tie-break instruction is just more context layered on top of the conflict. The contradiction is still there, and the stale rule keeps confusing Claude and humans.
whyWrong.B: Scoping a rule for a framework the repository no longer uses keeps wrong guidance alive. If Claude ever reads a file in those directories, the conflict comes straight back.
whyWrong.C: This is a heavy deterministic control for what is really a stale sentence, and it does nothing about the contradictory text still in context, which keeps confusing Claude and humans.

questions.mindset: Contradictory instructions are a configuration bug: delete the stale one rather than adding a referee.

questions.stem: A company has 300 developers working across more than 80 repositories. The compliance team wants a short set of data-handling reminders (for example, never put real customer records into test fixtures) present in every Claude Code session on company laptops, whatever repository is open. Individual developers must not be able to switch these reminders off. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Deploy the reminders as a managed policy CLAUDE.md at the OS's managed settings location, pushed to laptops by the company's device-management tooling.
Open a pull request against all 80 repositories that adds the reminders to each project CLAUDE.md, and require compliance approval for later changes.
Publish the reminders on the internal wiki and ask every developer to paste them into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md at onboarding and after each reinstall.
Put the reminders in a shared template repository's .claude/rules/ folder and ask teams to copy that folder whenever they create or update a repository.

questions.explanation: A **managed policy CLAUDE.md** (for example `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md` on macOS or `/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md` on Linux) applies to every user on the machine, in every repository, and **cannot be excluded by individual settings**. The docs suggest distributing it with MDM, Group Policy, Ansible or similar; the same content can also be delivered through the `claudeMd` key in managed settings. It is the documented home for compliance and data-handling guidance. If the requirement were to *block* an action, managed settings such as `permissions.deny` would be the right tool, but these are behavioral reminders.

whyWrong.B: This misses new repositories, needs 80 coordinated changes for every update, and a developer can skip project files with claudeMdExcludes, which cannot skip a managed CLAUDE.md.
whyWrong.C: User-level memory depends on each person doing it correctly, drifts over time, and can be edited or deleted by the developer, which breaks the must-not-switch-off requirement.
whyWrong.D: Copying folders between repositories drifts quickly, depends on each team remembering, and leaves the content fully under each team's control.

questions.mindset: Match the scope of the instruction to the scope of the requirement: org-wide and non-optional means managed policy.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code daily for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation in a shared repository, and you own how it is configured for the whole team.
questions.stem: An engineer on the payments team always starts Claude Code in monorepo/apps/payments-api, a Go service. An ancestor file, monorepo/apps/CLAUDE.md, is owned by the web platform team and contains long Next.js routing guidance that is useful for most apps but irrelevant to his service. It loads in every one of his sessions and sometimes leads Claude to suggest frontend patterns. He wants to stop loading that one file for himself without affecting anyone else. What should he do?

options.text: Delete the Next.js guidance from monorepo/apps/CLAUDE.md in a pull request, since the payments team's Go service has no use for it at all.
Add a claudeMdExcludes pattern for that file's path to his own local settings, such as .claude/settings.local.json in the repository.
Add a line to his CLAUDE.local.md telling Claude to ignore all routing guidance that comes from the web platform team's CLAUDE.md file.
Use @ imports in the payments-api CLAUDE.md to list only the files he wants, so that the other ancestor files are no longer loaded.

questions.explanation: Ancestor CLAUDE.md files load at launch. For large monorepos the docs provide **`claudeMdExcludes`**, a setting that skips specific CLAUDE.md files by path or glob pattern. It can be set at any settings layer (user, project, local or managed), so putting it in his **local** settings affects only him and leaves the file in place for the teams that need it.

whyWrong.A: That guidance is useful to other apps. Deleting it fixes his problem by breaking everyone else's, which violates the requirement to affect no one else.
whyWrong.C: This is a prompt-only fix: the irrelevant file still loads and uses context, and Claude now has to reconcile one instruction against another.
whyWrong.D: @ imports add files to context. They do not stop Claude Code from loading the ancestor CLAUDE.md files it already discovers.

questions.mindset: To stop something loading, use the loading control, not another instruction telling Claude to ignore it.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code daily for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation in a shared repository, and you own how it is configured for the whole team.
questions.stem: The team ran /init and now has a reasonable starter CLAUDE.md. In a planning meeting, engineers propose additions. The team wants to keep the file short and limit it to facts Claude would otherwise have to be told again in every session. Which TWO proposed entries are the BEST additions? Choose TWO.

options.text: A generated list of all dependencies in package.json with pinned versions, so that Claude knows which libraries exist.
A one-paragraph description of what each top-level source file does, regenerated whenever files are added or renamed.
"Integration tests only pass via make test-int, which starts the Postgres container first; npm test runs unit tests only."
The complete text of the team's 40-step quarterly release runbook, so that Claude can follow it whenever a release comes up.
"Money is stored as integer cents; the legacy amount_float column is read-only and must never be written to by any code path."

questions.explanation: The docs frame CLAUDE.md as the place to write down what you would otherwise re-explain: build and test commands, conventions, "always do X" rules and pitfalls, especially things that differ from tool defaults or that a code review keeps catching. Both correct options are short, checkable facts Claude **cannot derive from the code**: a non-default test command with its reason, and a data-handling rule that is a team decision rather than something visible in the schema. Content Claude can work out by reading the repository (dependency lists, file-by-file summaries, architecture overviews) adds context cost every session and goes stale; the `/doctor` trim check specifically proposes cutting it.

whyWrong.A: Claude can read package.json whenever it needs it. A pinned list costs context in every session and is out of date the moment any dependency changes.
whyWrong.B: File-by-file summaries are derivable from the code, drift as the codebase moves, and are exactly the kind of content the docs suggest trimming.
whyWrong.D: A long multi-step procedure that runs occasionally belongs in a skill, where it loads only when invoked. In CLAUDE.md it would bloat every session and still only run with Claude's judgment.

questions.mindset: CLAUDE.md is for what Claude cannot work out on its own and would otherwise be told every session.

questions.stem: A developer works in the orders-service repository and launches Claude Code with --add-dir ../platform-standards so Claude can read the shared standards repository. platform-standards contains its own CLAUDE.md with logging conventions and a .claude/skills/ folder with a scaffold-service skill. The developer notices Claude ignores the logging conventions. Which TWO statements are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: By default, CLAUDE.md files in a directory added with --add-dir are not loaded, which is why the logging conventions are missing from the session.
Listing ../platform-standards under permissions.additionalDirectories in settings.json would load both its CLAUDE.md and its skills automatically.
CLAUDE.md files from an added directory always load, but at lower priority, so the orders-service CLAUDE.md silently overrides them.
Setting CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1 when launching with --add-dir makes Claude Code load memory files from that directory.
Skills in the added directory's .claude/skills/ also stay unloaded until the same environment variable is set, just like its CLAUDE.md.

questions.explanation: `--add-dir` grants Claude access to directories outside the working directory, but **CLAUDE.md files from those directories are not loaded by default**. Setting `CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1` tells Claude Code to load them too. Skills behave differently: Claude Code loads the added directory's `.claude/skills/` (along with its commands and agents) without that variable.

whyWrong.B: permissions.additionalDirectories in settings.json grants file access only. It loads none of that directory's skills, commands, agents or memory files.
whyWrong.C: There is no lower-priority automatic load. The file simply isn't loaded by default, so nothing is being overridden.
whyWrong.E: Skills from an added directory load without the environment variable. The variable controls memory files only.

questions.mindset: File access and configuration loading are separate switches; know which one each mechanism flips.

questions.stem: A team created a project skill for writing database schema migrations. Its frontmatter description reads "Helpers for db stuff." When engineers ask "add a nullable archived_at column to the orders table", Claude writes an ad-hoc SQL file and never uses the skill, although typing the skill's name with a slash works fine. What is the MOST effective fix?

options.text: Rewrite the description to say what the skill does and when to use it, leading with words engineers say, such as migrations and columns.
Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude it must always use the skill for anything at all related to the database or SQL.
Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter so that it runs as an isolated subagent that Claude can delegate database work to more easily.
Set user-invocable: false in the skill's frontmatter so Claude treats it as background knowledge it should apply on its own.

questions.explanation: Claude decides whether to apply a skill from its **description** (plus `when_to_use`, if set), which is all it sees until the skill is invoked. "Helpers for db stuff" gives Claude nothing to match against. The docs' troubleshooting advice for a skill that doesn't trigger is to make sure the description includes the keywords users would naturally say, with the key use case first.

whyWrong.B: This uses always-on context to work around a bad description. Every session pays for it, and the blanket "anything database" rule may pull the skill into unrelated work.
whyWrong.C: context: fork changes where the skill runs once invoked. It does nothing to help Claude recognize when the skill is relevant.
whyWrong.D: This only hides the skill from the / menu and stops users from invoking it. Claude still matches on the same vague description.

questions.mindset: A skill's description is its trigger; write it for matching, not as a label.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your company runs Claude Code in its CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, propose test cases and post feedback. Developers only trust it if feedback is actionable and grounded in the actual change.
questions.stem: The pipeline invokes a /review-pr skill whose body begins: "First run git diff origin/main...HEAD, then review the changes against our checklist." In a few runs Claude reviewed a different range or skipped the command and reviewed files it had opened for other reasons, producing comments about code the PR never touched. The team wants the correct diff to be in front of Claude every single time, with minimal change. What should they do?

options.text: Add allowed-tools: Bash(git diff *) to the skill's frontmatter so that Claude can run the diff command without waiting for a permission prompt.
Add an IMPORTANT note at the top of the skill saying that Claude must run exactly this diff command first and review no other files.
Add context: fork to the skill so that the review runs in a fresh subagent with no access to files opened earlier in the job.
Replace the instruction with a !`git diff origin/main...HEAD` line so that its output is inserted into the skill before Claude sees it.

questions.explanation: The `` !`<command>` `` syntax is **dynamic context injection**: Claude Code runs the command when the skill is invoked and replaces the line with its output, so Claude receives the actual diff rather than an instruction it might follow differently. That turns a step Claude could skip or vary into something Claude Code does every time.

whyWrong.A: Pre-approving the command removes a prompt, but Claude still decides whether and how to run it, which is the source of the inconsistency.
whyWrong.B: Stronger wording is still a prompt-only fix for a step that can be made deterministic, and it is the approach that has already failed sometimes.
whyWrong.C: A forked subagent starts without the conversation history, but it still has to choose to run the command and can still pick the wrong range.

questions.mindset: If the data can be fetched deterministically, inject it rather than asking the model to go get it.

questions.stem: A team wrote a warehouse-allocation-context skill that explains how their 15-year-old warehouse system decides which bin to pick stock from. Claude should apply it automatically whenever someone works on allocation code. Engineers keep seeing it in the / menu, running it by hand, and getting a wall of background text with no action taken. What is the BEST change?

options.text: Set disable-model-invocation: true so that the skill only loads when someone deliberately types its name with a slash and never appears unprompted.
Move the entire skill body into the project CLAUDE.md so that the allocation explanation is loaded in context for every session.
Set user-invocable: false so that the skill is hidden from the / menu while Claude can still load it when allocation work is relevant.
Delete the skill's description field so that it no longer shows up with a summary in the menu engineers browse for commands.

questions.explanation: `user-invocable: false` is designed for **background knowledge** that isn't a meaningful command: Claude Code hides the skill from the `/` menu, but its description stays in context and Claude can still invoke it when relevant. The opposite flag, `disable-model-invocation`, is for side-effect workflows the user must start deliberately.

whyWrong.A: This is the opposite control: it stops Claude from invoking the skill on its own, which removes the automatic behavior the team wants.
whyWrong.B: It works, but it charges every session, including ones that never touch allocation code, for knowledge only that work needs.
whyWrong.D: Without a description Claude falls back to the first line of the body, which makes matching worse, and the skill would still be in the menu.

questions.mindset: Pick the invocation control by asking who should start it: the user, Claude, or both.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are building developer productivity tooling on Claude Code that helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks.
questions.stem: An engineer has long kept a personal skill at ~/.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md that deploys to his own sandbox. This week the platform team rolled out a managed deploy skill to every laptop through the managed settings directory. Since then, /deploy on his machine runs the company version and his sandbox steps never happen. He wants his version back for his own use without changing anything for other developers. What BEST explains the behavior and fixes it?

options.text: Personal skills normally win over every other location, so his SKILL.md frontmatter must have become malformed; he should fix the YAML and run /deploy again.
Skills are cached when a session starts, so his personal version will return once he restarts Claude Code after the managed rollout completed.
Both skills share a name and only one is listed, so he should add a line to his CLAUDE.local.md telling Claude to prefer his sandbox steps when /deploy runs.
An enterprise skill takes precedence over a personal skill with the same name, so he should rename his skill, e.g. to deploy-sandbox, and invoke it.

questions.explanation: When skills at the enterprise, personal and project levels share a name, the docs' resolution order is **enterprise over personal, and personal over project**. A skill deployed through the managed settings directory therefore shadows his `~/.claude/skills/deploy`. Giving his skill a distinct name keeps both available: `/deploy` for the company flow and `/deploy-sandbox` for his own, with nothing changed for anyone else.

whyWrong.A: The premise is reversed: enterprise skills outrank personal ones. A malformed frontmatter would still let /deploy-sandbox run by name, but it is not what happened here.
whyWrong.B: A restart doesn't change the precedence order. The enterprise skill still wins for the shared name after restarting.
whyWrong.C: This is a prompt-only workaround: the enterprise skill is the one that loads, and Claude is left reconciling an instruction against a procedure it was given. It also tempts Claude to alter a company-managed workflow.

questions.mindset: When a shared name suddenly resolves differently, check which scope outranks yours before editing anything.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your company runs Claude Code in its CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, propose test cases and post feedback. Developers only trust it if feedback is actionable and grounded in the actual change.
questions.stem: A license-check skill bundles a script at scripts/check-licenses.sh inside its own skill folder, and its body says "Run scripts/check-licenses.sh and report any violations." It works when the CI job starts Claude Code at the repository root, but fails with "No such file or directory" when a job starts it inside packages/api. What is the MOST reliable fix?

options.text: Copy the script into every package directory in the monorepo so the relative path resolves wherever the CI job happens to start Claude.
Reference the script as ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/check-licenses.sh in the skill body so it resolves from the skill's own folder.
Add a step telling Claude to search the repository with Glob for check-licenses.sh first, then run whichever matching file it finds.
Hard-code the CI runner's absolute checkout path to the script in the skill body so it no longer depends on the current directory.

questions.explanation: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` expands to the directory containing the skill's `SKILL.md`. The docs recommend it for referencing scripts or files bundled with a skill **regardless of the current working directory**. The same variable can also be used in an `allowed-tools` Bash rule, so the bundled script runs without a permission prompt.

whyWrong.A: Duplicating the script across packages creates many copies that drift apart, just to work around a path problem.
whyWrong.C: This adds a non-deterministic search step that could find the wrong file or a stale copy, where a substitution variable solves it exactly.
whyWrong.D: This breaks on developer machines and on any runner whose checkout path differs, and it has to be edited every time the CI layout changes.

questions.mindset: Make a skill self-contained: resolve its bundled files relative to the skill, not to wherever the session started.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code daily for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation in a shared repository, and you own how it is configured for the whole team.
questions.stem: A /safe-refactor skill contains two lines among its steps: "Run the tests" and "Never edit files under src/generated/". In the first response after invocation Claude follows both. Twenty turns later in the same session, Claude has edited two generated files and stopped running tests after its changes. The team considers the generated-files rule non-negotiable, while running the tests is good practice that Claude should apply as it works. Which TWO changes are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add a sentence at the end of SKILL.md asking Claude to re-read the skill file every few turns and confirm it is still following each step.
Enforce the generated-files rule with a PreToolUse hook, e.g. in the skill's hooks frontmatter, that blocks edits to src/generated/.
Set disable-model-invocation: true on the skill so the rules apply only when an engineer explicitly types /safe-refactor themselves.
Add allowed-tools: Edit Bash to the skill's frontmatter so the skill's own permissions limit what Claude can touch for the session.
Reword the testing step as a standing instruction covering the whole task, such as "Run the tests after every edit you make."

questions.explanation:
The skill's content enters the conversation once when invoked and **is not re-read on later turns**, so one-time phrasing like "Run the tests" reads as a single step. The docs split the fix by how strict the rule is:

- A rule that must hold every time belongs in a **hook**, which Claude Code runs on every matching event whether or not Claude is following the skill. Hooks can be defined in the skill's own `hooks` frontmatter; Claude Code registers them when the skill is invoked and keeps running them for the rest of the session.
- Guidance applied with judgment should be **worded to cover the whole task**, such as "Run the tests after every edit".

whyWrong.A: Asking the model to self-check is still prompt-only compliance for a non-negotiable rule, and it adds noise to every turn without guaranteeing anything.
whyWrong.C: This only changes who can start the skill. Once invoked, the same drift happens because nothing enforces the rules.
whyWrong.D: allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools for the invoking turn; it does not restrict other tools or block paths, so it cannot stop the edits.

questions.mindset: Must-always rules get deterministic enforcement; judgment rules get phrasing that lasts the whole task.

questions.stem: An engineer is writing a /scaffold-endpoint skill that takes a resource name and an HTTP method, for example /scaffold-endpoint "order items" POST. The body needs to use each value separately. Which TWO statements about passing arguments to this skill are correct? Choose TWO.

options.text: Indexed placeholders are zero-based, so $0 (or $ARGUMENTS[0]) receives the resource name and $1 (or $ARGUMENTS[1]) receives the HTTP method.
Indexed placeholders start at one, so $1 receives the resource name and $2 receives the HTTP method, just like positional shell arguments.
Arguments use shell-style quoting, so wrapping order items in quotes passes the two-word resource name to the skill as a single argument.
If the skill body contains no argument placeholder at all, Claude Code silently discards whatever the user typed after the skill name.
If the engineer passes only one argument, an unmatched $1 in the body expands to an empty string rather than staying in the text.

questions.explanation: Per the skills docs, `$ARGUMENTS[N]` accesses an argument by **0-based index**, and `$N` is shorthand for it, so `$0` is the first argument. Indexed arguments use **shell-style quoting**, so `"order items"` arrives as one value. `$ARGUMENTS` on its own still expands to the full string as typed.

whyWrong.B: The index is 0-based. With this layout $1 would receive the HTTP method, not the resource name.
whyWrong.D: When no placeholder receives the input, Claude Code appends ARGUMENTS: <your input> to the skill content so Claude still sees it.
whyWrong.E: An indexed placeholder with no matching argument stays in the content unchanged. Only named placeholders from the arguments frontmatter expand to empty.

questions.mindset: Know the exact substitution rules so a skill behaves predictably with every input shape.
